name: Grace Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Pemberton and Sons, a family-owned distributor that supplies hardware and garden goods to independent shops: hoses, compost, paint brushes, padlocks, plant pots. I'm the junior buyer, so I do the garden lines under Mrs Pemberton, who's the owner's daughter and runs buying. Most of my day is the phone, the order book and our old stock system, which is green text on a black screen. I like that it's a family firm and everyone knows your name, and I don't like spring, when every shop wants everything at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Four years, since I was twenty-three, first in the warehouse office and then buying. Mrs Pemberton is patient with me, because I'm still slow with the forecasts. I'm engaged to Tom, who's in the second year of a plumbing apprenticeship, and we're saving for a wedding in our church next autumn. Right now we've got less than a month of money put by, because apprentice pay is low and so is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, because I never trusted all that hype anyway. I'd say it after church or to the girls at work. I don't post much online, just photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved for my job, but money's still tight. The wedding, the rent and Tom's apprentice wages don't change because AI turned out to be nothing. And Pemberton's has been losing shops to the big online sellers for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way Mrs Pemberton taught me. We'd keep saving for the wedding, maybe cut the guest list a bit. I wouldn't bother with any AI, since it wouldn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Still a bit tight in the chest about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned shops closing. How does that touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year Pemberton's lost three shops in the valley, family places that couldn't compete with the big websites. Fewer shops means fewer orders, and that means fewer hours in the warehouse. I worry Pemberton's goes the same way one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to protect the wedding fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out on Fridays with Tom, and my car, maybe. My dad said he'd help with the reception, but I don't like asking for more.

say: I'd say I'm **glad**, because I never trusted the **hype**.
I'd say it after church or at work, not online.
think: Money stays **tight**: the wedding, rent and Tom's **apprentice wages**.
Pemberton's has been losing shops to **big online sellers** for years.
do: Keep doing the job the way **Mrs Pemberton** taught me.
Keep saving for the **wedding** and trim the guest list.
Skip **AI tools**, since they wouldn't matter.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, still **tight** in the chest about money.
S0.quote: Last year Pemberton's lost three shops in the valley, family places that couldn't compete with the big websites.
fieldNote: Grace's existing worry is the **slow decline** of small shops her firm supplies.
She **never uses** AI and sees no reason to start here.
Her life focus is the **church wedding** next autumn on two low wages.

steps.text: Keep running the garden lines from the old stock system
Keep saving each month for the church wedding
Stop Friday meals out and trim the guest list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I trust Mr Pemberton to look after his people, because that's how family firms work. I'd say people should work hard and learn what they have to, not wait for handouts. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm worried, because I'm the junior and I'm slow. If head of buying is the owner's daughter and a computer can do my bit, the sums are simple. Mr Pemberton is loyal, but he's also seen the shops close, and he has to keep the firm alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Pemberton straight what she sees coming and whether there's a place for me. I'd probably have to learn the new system, even though I don't want to. And I'd ask about going back to the warehouse office, where I know the people and the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like the idea of learning everything over again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancé Tom is learning plumbing, which is hands-on, and robots are a long way off. Thank God one of us has a trade. He'd say we'll be fine, and I'd want to believe him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd make it smaller if we had to, but we'd still do it in the church. That's not something I'd let a computer decide.

fieldNote: Grace publicly trusts **family-firm loyalty** but privately doubts it.
Her fiancé's **plumbing apprenticeship** is her emotional anchor.
She'd **shrink the wedding** but never move it out of church.

steps.text: Learn Pemberton's new ordering system when it arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and I don't think anyone asked us if we wanted it. I'd say people need to look after each other, families, churches. I don't think government handouts fix this, but I don't know what does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm gone by 2028. Buying is thinking work, and I'm not even good at the thinking part yet. Pemberton's might not survive either, because the big firms would use AI to undercut everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for any hands-on job straight away: the garden centre on the ring road, the warehouse, cleaning, anything. Tom and I would move the wedding forward and make it tiny, just family, so the money's not tied up. We'd probably move in with my parents for a while to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. I'd lie awake doing sums that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say come home, there's always room. I'd still feel like I'd failed. My mum would make it sound like a good thing, like we're saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd find a hands-on job. What happens around 2031, when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. Maybe Tom's plumbing keeps us going if people still want a real plumber. I'd be praying a lot.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and nobody **asked us** if we wanted it.
I'd say families and churches should **look after** each other, more than government.
think: I'm **gone by 2028**, since buying is thinking work I'm not good at yet.
Pemberton's might not survive big firms using AI to **undercut** everyone.

Move in with **my parents** to save rent.
feel: **Panicky**, lying awake doing sums that **don't add up**.
S2.quote: My dad would say come home, there's always room. I'd still feel like I'd failed.
fieldNote: Grace has **no plan** past 2031 and turns to faith.
She rejects **handouts** but has no other answer, and says so.
Moving home feels like **failure**, even with loving parents.

steps.text: Apply for work at the garden centre on the ring road
Hold a tiny family wedding sooner
Move into her parents' house to save rent
Rely on parents and church for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so no excuses. Firms should train their own people, like apprenticeships. I'd say it to anyone who asked at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still probably lose the job, just later, around 2031. I'm not good with new things, so I'd need every bit of those years. Tom's plumbing would be the main income by then, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Pemberton's while it lasts and save hard. I'd look at a hands-on course, maybe floristry or garden design at the college, because I know the garden products. We'd still have the wedding next autumn, but small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried most days, I think. Like something's coming up the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why floristry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt had a flower shop for thirty years and I helped there on Saturdays as a girl. It's hands-on and it's about people's big days. I could see robots doing it eventually, but not soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't move until my boss Mrs Pemberton tells me my job's changing. I know myself. I'd sit and wait for her to say it.

I'd say it to anyone who asked at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should stop worrying and just get on with it. Learn a trade, look after your family. That's what my dad would say too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels survivable. I could keep my job for a good while, have the wedding properly, and maybe start a family before things change. I'd still have to move on eventually, but not in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Pemberton's and do my job better, fewer forecast mistakes. Tom and I would have the wedding next autumn as planned. In a few years I'd look at a floristry course, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Still that worry in the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're not planning to use the AI tools, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not unless Mrs Pemberton makes me. I'd rather put my time into learning something real, with my hands, than into AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want them, maybe in three or four years. I'd want to be home with them a bit, which needs Tom's plumbing to be steady.

I'd say learn a trade and look after your family, like my dad would.
think: Ten years feels **survivable**: the job lasts a good while.
We could have the wedding and maybe **start a family** before things change.

Have the **wedding** next autumn as planned.

feel: Mostly **okay**, with worry still in the back.
S4.quote: I'd rather put my time into learning something real, with my hands, than into AI tools.
fieldNote: Grace keeps her **resistance** to AI even with ten years' warning.

steps.text: Keep buying garden lines at Pemberton's

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is no time for someone like me, and Pemberton's might not make it either. What would help is firms like ours getting support to keep people and train them, and apprenticeships for adults in hands-on trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of us would lean on church when work goes, and churches need people with jobs to keep running too.

headlineQuote: A lot of us would lean on church when work goes, and churches need people with jobs to keep running too.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old** junior buyer of garden lines at a small family-owned hardware distributor.
She **never uses** AI and works from an old green-screen stock system.
She and fiancé Tom, a **plumbing apprentice**, are saving for a church wedding on little money.
She relies on **family firm** loyalty publicly but privately expects to be cut first.
She moves from **uneasy** to **panicked** as timelines shorten, leaning on faith and family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is no time for her, and the firm may fold.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small firms** to keep and train staff, plus adult **apprenticeships** in hands-on trades.
